pitch_detail.notes: Start by standing on the right-hand tongue sticking out of an overlap, then take the grainy crack. A bulging crack comes next, after which you step right to the clear left-facing corner system and follow it up and leftward. Belay in gray rock where multiple crack systems meet.

Go up the crack overhead, angling left, and move harder left when ledges show up, to a belay in the big left-facing corner of The Knobivore. From there, either traverse mostly leftward to easy ground, or keep climbing the corner until you can go left to the roof of Better Than the Alternative.

review.changed: Wrote the 2 pitches described; no grades or lengths stated. Text calls them short and says about 250 ft of climbing precedes the gray rock band.
review.other_findings: Row says 4 pitches; text describes 2 short pitches to the ledge system.

pitch_detail.notes: Cracks lead to a left-facing corner; stay in that corner where The Alternative veers left. Hand-jam the corner that changes direction, tiptoe over gray rock to the orange bulge, step right of the large horn and pull into the orange. Continue to a stance where many cracks converge just under a corner about 20 ft high, orange on its right.
Climb the corner (the crux), then face climb above it, drifting left to a stance where cracks cut up through the big overlap/corner system that leans right. Short pitch.

Cracks through the overlap are harder than they appear. Then face climb up and left to the giant overlap/corner that curves back right, go up it and through the steep overlap, and belay on a stance at cracks.
Climb cracks, edge right along the ledge system, then up again to reach the notch/gully.
The gully above quickly eases to 3rd class. Walk and scramble back to easy ground at the northwest end of the East Face formation.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with lengths from feet; none of them graded in the text.

pitch_detail.notes: Trend up and left along cracks, passing over the line of Better Than the Alternative, into a wide crack system that keeps heading left. The belay sits under a pair of cracks that hold a precarious hanging block.

Cross the overlap using the cracks, or holds on the face if you favour those. Afterward meander up and left, choosing the simplest weaknesses or jug-filled face, to a stance that barely works at the foot of a right-facing corner.
Take the corner to easier ground.

Scramble 3rd class along the ridge, then descend by traversing down on the west side to a sandy area. Carry on north, on the crest itself or on slabs just east of it, until a few downclimbing moves and a short gully reach level ground.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches; no grades or lengths stated.

pitch_detail.notes: After scrambling the low-angle southwest ramp (belays are plentiful), head straight for the obvious roof, which is the crux. Good hand holds get you over it. Then move left to a crack, taking care with loose knobs, that ends on a roomy ledge where a detached block sits.
Take the crack right above to a further ledge, then an easy scramble reaches the summit.

rappel_detail.station: summit anchor: a single bolt plus a fixed piece
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel back to the ledge below. The remaining descent down the chasm between Peaks 8 and 9 is a short 4th class downclimb, not a rappel. A 60 m rope is recommended.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches and the single rappel station the text lists; the second descent step is a downclimb, so it is not a rappel entry.

pitch_detail.notes: Rope up at large vertical flakes on the lowest toe left of the huge chimney/chasm. Broken ledges lead to a notable right-facing corner system; follow it until a wide crack (a #4 BD fits) appears, climb that, then traverse right to a bolted anchor sitting beneath a shallow corner system that faces left.

Two bolts and tricky 5.10 moves lead to a horn you mantle. Ledges follow, then a thin flake on the left that you lieback through two bolts (crux) to a ledge. Climb an easier splitter to another ledge, then right and up to a bolted anchor in front of a big chimney behind a flake.

Enter the chimney, passing two chockstones that are both sound; the first is graceful, the second awkward. Next comes a superb hand crack, on the right, in a corner facing right that contains a flake. At the top go left, then up and back right to a bolted anchor.

Follow the ramp leftward from the anchor and mantle. Then pick one: climb the flake's right side directly (a fingers corner), or detour left around it and use cracks beyond (simpler, but with an awkward leftward move). On top of the large flake, friction traverse right with care, rising to ledges and a bolted anchor beneath the big crack system above.

Step into the left-facing corner system above the belay. Its first 5 m are technical 5.10 with two bolts, and small cracks in the right wall help your feet. Climbing eases beneath a roof; place a solid cam, go around the roof's left side, and mantle to a sloping ledge. Fine splitter hands follow to a good stance at a pillar. The anchor is just one bolt beside a pillar you can sling.

Stay on the splitter; as the crack narrows, perfect footholds appear and take you to a small sloping ledge. Then use #3s and #4s in the wider crack (one bolt offers a rest while leap-frogging the #4) until it kinks left to an exposed belay on stacked blocks. Build the anchor at the far end.

The rock changes character here and the angle drops slightly. It is fused and sturdier than it looks, but stay alert. Go up and left, first along a groove, then to the arete, with a few concerning moves to a good sandy ledge.

Enter the big chimney/slot above and aim for a giant chockstone 20 m up; take care. Stem over it on good gear. Beyond, a choice: left into a steep rubbly gully of questionable rock, or right into cleaner but harder-looking cracks. Heading right toward the tallest pinnacle ends on the true summit. Either way you finish within 5 m of the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with lengths and grades. Anchors stated only for P1-P5 (bolted).
review.other_findings: None. The text notes the three hard sections (5.11- crux and two 5.10 bits) are short enough to aid through.

pitch_detail.notes: Reach the big ledge with the tree; begin on its far right at the highest point. A nice crack leads up to the ledge.

Take the right-hand corner of the three big ones. The opening boulder problem has two bolts. The tight corner takes varied crack techniques and is the technical crux. Leave it on the right and end at a great belay ledge on the left (bolted). Good enough as a single-pitch crag climb.
Go up the right-facing corner and belay in the alcove.

Climb the right-hand crack, then traverse right along the wide crack under the roof (a burly crux). Next the chimney, then up through red rock and left to a bolted anchor, where the second crux is loose rock.
Move carefully up the dihedral, clipping a bolt to its right, then continue on steep blocky double cracks to a bolted anchor.
Pass two bolts heading to the huge chockstone, leave to the right along the roof crack, and go roughly 20 ft higher to set an anchor in the corner.
Up the corner and out right through an exciting exit, then belay about 10 ft below the slab.
Wander up the slab toward the main weakness on the left and belay at the foot of the last wide splitter crack.
The final crack, reaching the ridge crest and easier ground. Then 4th class to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches. No rappel table: rappelling is described only in general (bolted anchors from the top of pitch 5 with two ropes; pitch 1 from the tree or the two bolts).
review.other_findings: descent_text null on the row; the text gives a walk-off: scramble down the northwest side and work clockwise back to the base. New alpine route: expect some loose rock and lichen.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy ground leads up and left to a belay in a corner.
Climb the corner, traverse right on the face to a crack, and follow it to a roof, exiting left beneath the roof.

The right-facing corner, clean and fine. The first ascent effort was 5.12 but with cleaning it should settle near 5.11 (moss about 5 ft thick still sits in it). Belay in the corner after the difficult part.
Finish the corner, then cross a slab to the right to belay on a small arete.
Steeper, more broken rock to the base of a right-facing corner.
Climb the corner and follow cracks up to the ridge crest, where the route joins the Beckey North Arete. Scramble to the base of pitch 7.
Climb flakes just right of two large corners; this stretch is also part of the Beckey North Arete route. Fourth class then leads to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches; no lengths or anchors stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Take one of the cracks on the slab's left side, whichever line reaches the double-cracked roof. High on the pitch, move left to avoid a grungy squeeze and use another crack to cross a small roof (5.8).
The crack continues through the double-cracked roof with big jugs (5.8), then widens up to the top of the slab.

Move the belay over flat easy ground for roughly 50 ft, rounding the left-hand corner of a face to the buttress edge, where a deep gully drops on the left. Follow that left edge on nice hand cracks and features (5.8), then work out right onto a featured face finishing at a comfortable belay inside a shallow diagonal gully.

Continue up the shallow diagonal gully toward a notch on the buttress's left edge, climb up and out of the gully (5.6), and keep going to the buttress top. Easy fifth class, then fourth class, reaches the base of a short face split by vertical cracks.
A perfect hand crack goes up the short face for 30 ft (5.7); easy fourth class beyond leads to the summit ridge.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches with lengths in metres as stated.

pitch_detail.notes: A clean crack through a scoop leads to the foot of an excellent hand-fist crack. Can be linked with the next pitch. Graded 5.8 to 5.9.
The evident hand and fist crack to a ledge.
Above the ledge an arching crack continues; a thin boulder problem briefly breaks up the hand crack. After topping out the shield, carry on along the ridge.
Ridge climbing, with optional crack boulder problems on the gendarmes. Those can be skirted to the right for far easier going. Graded 5.8 to 5.10.
Continue up the ridge and finish with a brief off-width to the summit. Grade given as 5.8 to 5.9.

review.changed: Wrote 5 entries covering the 7 pitches the text condenses (4-5 and 6-7 combined as the text gives them); grade ranges kept in notes. The text says the pitching is approximate.

pitch_detail.notes: A flaring but clean hand crack up to where the angle eases and the terrain turns to ledges. Anchor with finger-size pieces around the boulder you see straight ahead after topping out.
Scramble 4th class terrain up to the summit of the ridge. Roped or unroped is your choice, though a fall would be quite serious. Avoid kicking loose rocks down.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Route can serve as an exit or extension to Corn Silk.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the left-facing corner, then the hand crack that trends left up the arete/face and over a small roof, finishing at a sloping ledge with a belay of two bolts. A start further left on the finger crack, hand-traversing into that same corner, is also possible.
Go up the corner to a stance, stem up and right, then step around the arete on its left. Cracks reach a nice ledge under a hand/fist crack, with a gear belay.
Hand/fist crack into a steep thin-hands crack, then the left-facing corner through a roof, exiting on its right. Build a belay on a ledge below the wide right-facing corner.
The right-facing corner through blocky ledges, to a comfortable ledge belay.
Easy ridge climbing, low 5th class, all the way up to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 5 entries for 6 pitches (5 and 6 are described as one stretch of ridge).

pitch_detail.notes: Lieback a corner system facing left, with good rests, until you reach a small ledge. Above it, a steep corner facing left holds a small roof and a bolt; pass the roof, then work right and upward over a flake system past a second bolt. The wider flake above ends at a belay on a nice ledge. Graded 5.10+ or 5.11a.

The dagger pitch, full of roofs. Climb up and right, then left under a small roof (bolt on its lip). Continue up and left, clinging and laybacking around a bigger roof, with a great knee bar to rest on. Lieback flakes that face left to a small roof, step right out of it onto the face and back left to the arete past a bolt. Arete and corner finish on top of the dagger at an exposed belay.
Finger crack using the arete of a left-facing corner, into a left-facing corner system; follow it over into an alcove and belay.
The hand crack right of the belay leads into the roof; finger crack through the roof, then the face, finishing on juggy flakes to a big ledge.
Hand crack in the right-facing corner, then hand and finger cracks up the face to a large ledge and gear belay.
Walk left along the ledge, then cracks to the ridge and a gear belay.
Ridge scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches with grades and lengths as stated.

pitch_detail.notes: The V-shaped crack, a double lieback. Leave it to the left, then return right at a bolt. Two protection bolts.
Featured cracks and face to a good stance, one protection bolt. Linking with the first pitch is worthwhile.

The crack continues up to steeper edges and a corner; step right to a ledge. Two protection bolts. A bolt with a line leaving left from the middle of this pitch belongs to a project still being worked, so skip it.
Groove to flake to groove, six protection bolts.
Superb 5.10 flakes and hand cracks, ending in a fingers corner. A step left past a bolt, which is tricky, gains an exposed stance. One protection bolt.
Slab around to the left to a splitter finger crack, over a small roof, and a hand crack to the end. Three protection bolts.
Up and right to a flare/corner, then up and left past a ledge, then up and right to another bolted anchor.
Ramble alpine-style to the top of the white rock.
A last stretch climbs red rock to the face's top; the rock is poorer, but the views of Whitney and beyond are worth it.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches with grades, lengths (feet to metres), bolt counts stated. No rappel table: only 'rappel the route', all anchors two bolts with links.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble 3rd class ledges, then climb downward-pointing flakes to a corner crack system (or a wider arching crack); either goes to the top of the pillar and a bolted belay.
A tricky smooth V slot/alcove through the reddish band up to a clear horn, where a big move left gains another crack system; follow it to a second leftward move and the next bolted anchor.

The crack goes straight up from the belay until flakes fill it; then look left and make a delicate traverse across to the prominent crystal tower, which stands at the foot of an airy, flying-style arete.

From the tower ledge step right into the corner and climb it, using the wide crack inside and the thin crack on its left wall to push past 3 or 4 bushes that complicate the crux. Beyond them, step left onto a good ledge and take a wide crack with plenty of face features to a still better ledge with a bolted belay.
Go right of the belay and follow cracks through another reddish band to a flared hand crack, ending on a ledge with a bolted belay.

Step left off the bolts and take the wide crack, which stays wide for only 10 or 15 ft before flakes allow narrower techniques. It continues past several small ledges into one more reddish band. A bolted anchor is there, but moving right onto easier ground and building a gear anchor on larger ledges is recommended.

Take the path of least resistance back left over easy ground, favouring the ramps and ledges of the white pillar's conical top and avoiding its major corner and the red headwall. Build a gear belay anywhere.
Continue across and up through many ledges, mostly easy with many options. A bolted anchor exists but may be hard to find and is not needed.

More wandering by the easiest line over corners and ledges, heading for the pillar's summit. The last bolted anchor is on the pillar top's right; stop there when rappelling, or climb about 40 ft more of red headwall to the west ridge crest.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches with grades, lengths (feet to metres) and bolted anchors where stated. No rappel table (rappel Civilized is an alternative; stations not listed here).

pitch_detail.notes: Many variations reach the first belay. One line starts in a left-facing finger-crack dihedral to a ledge, then goes right to a right-facing hand crack, veering slightly left to a small alcove with a roof (that roof has a hand crack on its right) and a protected belay spot. Grade given as 5.7 to 5.8. Rock quality is very good.

Mostly 5.8-5.9 except for the crux. A hand crack goes straight up, alternating tight, slot and wide hands, and takes both nuts and cams, with plenty of face holds. Higher it is interrupted by an undercling flake, which is the crux: traverse right and up on face holds (some protection) to a new tight-hands crack system, then straight up to the ridge. Belay on blocks; a black Alien and micro offset cam help. Length is about 60-65 m. Mostly solid rock with a few friable chips and flexing flakes.
The rock deteriorates sharply here. Go up and left toward the gully, follow it for a while, then turn left and straight up to the summit. Loose; step carefully.

review.changed: Wrote all 3 pitches; P1 and P2 ranges kept in notes, P2 length is a range so not set.

pitch_detail.notes: Also the first pitch of Blood of the Monkey. Begin in the evident right-facing dihedral on the needle's right side. When about 20 ft under the square-cut roof, move right onto face holds to a bolt under the roof; easier beyond. Trend up and right until a belay ledge shows on the left. Length is 40-60 m depending on the glacier snow level at the base.
The obvious right-facing corner above; the last 20 ft can be skipped by stepping left and following face holds to the ledge.

The Great White Shield. Take the crack left of and above the belay past a small overhang, then the superb splitter for about 100 ft until it dies out. Clip a bolt, then the slab traverse to the right is the crux, ending at the anchor.
Left-trending double cracks, then easier ground with a bolt, to a short finger crack followed by 2 bolts to the belay.

Lost at Seams. Thin seams, with a few bolts and small cams. About 10 ft past the top bolt (on the right), set small cams and stretch far to the left to an easy 3-inch crack; follow it 15 ft to a face bolt, then 15 ft more into a trough/hand crack trending left. Leave it for big orange flakes up the vertical wall to a bolt, then moderate face (5.8 R) until a flared crack with protection reaches the belay ledge.
X Marks the Spot. A tricky bolted undercling, then easier cracks into the evident steep right-facing dihedral that ends at Ammon's Ledge, the route's finest bivy ledge.
Release the Kraken. Bolted bouldery start to the large flake, then right up the steep, pumpy flake to the Crow's Nest belay ledge.
The Crow's Nest. Up a steep orange corner, then easier ground to the left of two major crack systems; follow the moderate 5.9 crack for 30 m to the belay out right.
Mile's Crack. Ascend the moderate crack again to the foot of the clear orange splitter on the vertical wall, and climb the splitter, which Blood of the Monkey also uses.
Captain Reach. Bolted seam and face, one hard crank, then fantastic pumpy climbing that eases to a belay mid-headwall.

The Gemstone Crack, among the finest pitches in the High Sierra: the splitter up the headwall's middle, protected by gear. Past the hard climbing, two bolts cover the last traverse right to the belay.
Cracks lead out right from the belay and finish below the orange chimney you can see above.
Climb the blocky chimney for 100 ft; when it becomes loose and very easy (4th class), step left to a clean splitter or thin hand crack that goes to a bolted belay at the foot of Harding Ledge.
The long-established exit pitch above Harding Ledge: a right-facing corner crack.
Finish on the upper part of the Harding Route to the summit, using that route's topo.

review.changed: Wrote 15 entries covering the 17 pitches (15-17 combined, as the text refers to the Harding topo). All belays stated bolted. No rappel table: only 'two 60 m ropes' is given.

pitch_detail.notes: Laybacking from the ground leads to a good tips corner; place the black totems high and layback/stem up to the bolt-protected layback crux, rest, then a good hands/fists splitter goes to a two-bolt belay. Double rack and one draw.

Climb left on easy ground to the sharp arete and use laybacks and sidepulls on either side of it. A bolt-protected crux comes at a deadpoint to a good jug; shake out with no feet, then more exposed laybacking. 7 draws.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches. No rappel table: only two single-rope rappels, stations not described.
review.other_findings: None; stored descent says single-rope rappel, consistent.
